bodyHtml:
The Hanunó'o script is an indigenous script used to write the Hanunó'o language, spoken on Mindoro Island, northeast of Palawan Province of The Philippines. Traditionally, Hanunó'o was written by carving characters into strips of bamboo; consequently, it is written vertically (up and down), as opposed to horizontally like the English alphabet.

Below on the left is a list of Filipino place names written in Hanunó'o in random order. On the right is the same list in Latin script, in a different order. Note that there are two extra cities in the Latin list!

  • A. Manila
  • B. Lubang
  • C. Rumbang
  • D. Paluan
  • E. Kaingal
  • F. Marikit
  • G. Pasig
  • H. Magsikap
  • I. Tubili
  • J. Mimaropa
  • K. Sablayan

H1. Determine the correct correspondences.

H2. Write the following Hanunó'o words in the Latin script.

H3. Write the following words in the Hanunó'o script:

  • 15. manuk
  • 16. bilawan
  • 17. nagsirung
  • 18. bais

questions.partPrompt: Determine the correct correspondences. For each Hanunó'o name 1-9, give the letter (A-K) of the matching name in the Latin list.
Write the following Hanunó'o words (10-14 in the second table) in the Latin script.

Write the following words in the Hanunó'o script. Since the handwritten script cannot be typed here, describe your spelling instead: list the letters in reading order (bottom to top), naming each letter's consonant and saying whether it carries a vowel mark for i or u, or a padmudpod (the hook that means no vowel).
questions.answerKey: Three letters, bottom to top: ma; na with the mark for u (nu); ka with a padmudpod, i.e. bare k.
Four letters, bottom to top: ba with the mark for i (bi); la; wa; na with a padmudpod, i.e. bare n.
Five letters, bottom to top: na; ga with a padmudpod (bare g); sa with the mark for i (si); ra with the mark for u (ru); nga with a padmudpod (bare ng).
Three letters, bottom to top: ba; the standalone letter for i; sa with a padmudpod, i.e. bare s.

hints.text: Each column is one name, but the script does not run the way you expect: it reads bottom to top. Before worrying about the shapes, compare how many separate letter-shapes a column has with how many consonants a candidate name has.

The script is an abugida: one plain letter stands for a consonant plus the vowel a. A short line written above or below a letter switches that vowel to i or u, and a small curved hook at the letter's bottom right (called padmudpod) means the consonant has no vowel at all. So a name whose only vowel is a will show no extra lines, and a name that ends in a consonant will show the hook on its topmost letter. The vowels a and i also have their own standalone letters when they are not attached to a consonant.

Try the method on a word that is not asked about, say kilala. Break it into ki-la-la, so three letters, written bottom to top: the ka letter with a line above it (making ki), then la, then la. No hooks appear, because no consonant is left vowel-less. Doing exactly this bookkeeping - number of letters, which ones carry an i or u line, which ones carry a hook - for every name in the Latin list is what lets you tell the columns apart.

explanationHtml:
What kind of writing system is this?

Hanunó'o is an abugida: instead of one symbol per sound, one full letter stands for a whole consonant-plus-vowel syllable, and the default vowel is a. Small extra marks adjust that vowel:

  • a plain letter = consonant + a (for example the ma letter);
  • a short line above or below the letter changes the vowel to i or u;
  • a small curved hook at the bottom right of the letter (its Hanunó'o name is padmudpod) means the consonant has no vowel at all;
  • the vowels a and i have their own standalone letters when they stand alone in a word.

The other surprise is the direction. The columns are read bottom to top, so the lowest letter in a column is the first sound of the name.

Step 1: count the letters each name would need

You do not need to recognise a single shape to get started. Break each Latin name into syllables and see how many letters it would take. Every consonant gets a letter, even a final one (it just wears the hook).

Latin nameSpelled outLetters
Manilama + ni + la3
Lubanglu + ba + ng(hook)3
Rumbangru + m(hook) + ba + ng(hook)4
Paluanpa + lu + a + n(hook)4
Kaingalka + i + nga + l(hook)4
Marikitma + ri + ki + t(hook)4
Pasigpa + si + g(hook)3
Magsikapma + g(hook) + si + ka + p(hook)5
Tubilitu + bi + li3
Mimaropami + ma + ro + pa4
Sablayansa + b(hook) + la + ya + n(hook)5

In the picture, columns 1 and 2 are the only ones with five letters, columns 5, 6 and 8 have three, and columns 3, 4, 7 and 9 have four. Since there are four three-letter names but only three three-letter columns, and five four-letter names but only four four-letter columns, exactly one of the extras is a three-letter name and one is a four-letter name.

Step 2: the two long names

Magsikap and Sablayan both need five letters, so they are columns 1 and 2 in some order. Look at the vowels: every vowel in Sablayan is a, so its column carries no i- or u-lines at all, only two hooks. Magsikap contains an i (in si), so its column must show one extra line. Column 1 has that line, column 2 does not: 1 = Magsikap (H), 2 = Sablayan (K).

A useful cross-check: the bottom letter of column 1 is the ma letter, and the same shape appears at the bottom of the columns for Manila and Marikit and of word 11 and 12 in the second table.

Step 3: the three-letter columns

Tubili has u on the first letter and i on the second and third, and no hook, because it ends in a vowel. Manila has an i only on its middle letter and no hook. Pasig ends in a consonant, so its top letter takes the hook, and its middle letter takes an i-line. Lubang would need a u-line on the bottom letter plus a hook on top. Matching these fingerprints against columns 5, 6 and 8 gives 5 = Tubili (I), 6 = Manila (A), 8 = Pasig (G) - and nothing is left for Lubang, so it is one of the two extra cities.

Step 4: the four-letter columns

Marikit needs two i-lines in the middle and a hook on top. Kaingal is the one that uses the standalone i letter as its second letter, plus a hook on top. Paluan uses the standalone a letter as its third letter, with a u-line on the second and a hook on top. Rumbang has a u-line on its bottom letter and two hooks. Mimaropa would need an i-line on the bottom letter and no hooks at all. The columns give 3 = Rumbang (C), 4 = Paluan (D), 7 = Marikit (F), 9 = Kaingal (E), so Mimaropa is the second extra.

H2: reading the script back into Latin letters

Now that you know the letters, read each column from the bottom up and add the vowel each mark calls for:

  • 10: two letters, ka then ng with a hook, so kang.
  • 11: ma, na with an i-line, ma with an i-line, sa with a u-line, so manimisu.
  • 12: ma, ng with a hook, ya, na with a hook, so mangyan.
  • 13: sa with an i-line, ba with a u-line, ya, na with a hook, so sibuyan.
  • 14: pa, la, wa, na with a hook, so palawan.

H3: writing new words

Go the other way: syllabify, then stack the letters bottom to top.

  • manuk = ma + nu (the na letter with a u-line) + bare k (the ka letter with a padmudpod): three letters.
  • bilawan = bi + la + wa + bare n: four letters.
  • nagsirung = na + bare g + si + ru + bare ng: five letters.
  • bais = ba + the standalone i letter + bare s: three letters. The vowel i here follows another vowel, so it cannot ride on a consonant letter and needs its own.

Answers to H1

1 = H, 2 = K, 3 = C, 4 = D, 5 = I, 6 = A, 7 = F, 8 = G, 9 = E. The two unused Latin names are B (Lubang) and J (Mimaropa).
_reviewNotes:
H1 and H2 answer keys are copied from the official solution page (1. H, 2. K, 3. C, 4. D, 5. I, 6. A, 7. F, 8. G, 9. E; 10. kang, 11. manimisu, 12. mangyan, 13. sibuyan, 14. palawan). H3 in the booklet requires drawing Hanunó'o glyphs, which cannot be typed: the four H3 questions have been reworded to ask for a bottom-to-top description of the letters and marks, graded by LLM. The official solution shows the drawn forms for 15-18; a reviewer may prefer to add the solution image as a reference. Point split is my own (H1 0.5 each = 4.5, H2 1.1 each = 5.5, H3 1.25 each = 5, total 15); the booklet gives no per-part breakdown. Figure crops need checking.
